detailed_rationale:
[DATA] CMS Info Systems is India's largest cash-logistics player -- roughly 46% share of the ATM cash-management business, ~36% of retail cash management, ~26% of cash-in-transit, and by the company's own claim it moves more than half of all physical cash circulating in the country across ~70,000 ATMs serviced. FY26 was, on the numbers, a genuinely bad year for this franchise, not a market overreaction to a clean print: consolidated revenue grew just 2.6% YoY to Rs 2,487 crore (services revenue +5.8% to Rs 2,312 crore), full-year EBITDA fell 5.2% to Rs 600 crore (margin down to 24.1%), and PAT dropped 18.5% YoY to Rs 303 crore. The proximate causes are identifiable and largely one-off/transitional rather than a steady-state repricing of the business: (1) the SBI integrated cash-solutions contract -- a Rs 1,000 crore, 10-year deal for ~5,000 ATMs -- kept getting pushed back (management cites a ~Rs 150 crore FY26 revenue hit) after CMS had already sunk capex into routes/infrastructure ahead of a go-live that slipped from roughly February to April to December before finally starting; (2) a contraction in the offsite-ATM market tied to competitor AGS Transact's distress/exit, which disrupted volumes industry-wide even though it should be share-accretive for CMS longer term as the remaining large-scale player; and (3) an abnormal wage step-up from a long-term employee settlement. Working-capital quality also genuinely deteriorated -- receivable days rose to 131 from 123, working-capital days more than doubled YoY, and once you count the ~Rs 190 crore spent on two bolt-on acquisitions (Securens Systems, an AIoT remote-monitoring leader, and FSS's ATM business) as investing outflow, headline free cash flow turned negative for the year even though operating cash flow (Rs 390 crore) still covered PAT comfortably at ~129%, in line with FY24-25.

The more important question for an existing holding is whether these drivers are now largely behind the company, and the evidence leans yes. The SBI contract went live in January 2026 and is now a locked-in Rs 1,000 crore/10-year revenue stream -- the single biggest swing factor in FY26's miss is resolved, not merely promised. Q4 FY26 already shows the inflection: services revenue crossed Rs 600 crore for the first time (+5.5% QoQ, the strongest sequential print in eight quarters), EBITDA margin expanded 280bp QoQ to 25.6%, and PAT rose 38% QoQ to Rs 79 crore. Management's FY27 guidance -- total revenue of Rs 2,800-2,900 crore (13-17% growth) and services revenue of Rs 2,700-2,800 crore (17-21% growth), with margins held near 25% -- is a credible return to the double-digit growth this business used to post (3-year revenue CAGR of 9.1% before the FY26 air-pocket). Capital allocation signals read as confidence rather than distress: the balance sheet remains net-cash (Rs 610 crore cash/investments against Rs 221 crore of newly-raised acquisition debt), the company just completed a Rs 167.93 crore tender-offer buyback (3% of equity at Rs 340/share) that was oversubscribed 9.07x, and it paid a combined Rs 5.25/share FY26 dividend. The PE-sponsor overhang that many investors worried about is also now history rather than a live risk -- Baring Private Equity Asia's vehicle (Sion Investment Holdings) has fully exited its stake (down to 0% by mid-2025) via block sales, and CEO Rajiv Kaul has since raised his own personal holding from ~2.6% to ~6.2%, an insider-alignment signal running the opposite direction of a typical promoter-exit red flag.

On the structural question -- is cash logistics a shrinking TAM being priced honestly, or a temporarily-out-of-favor compounder -- the data doesn't support an imminent collapse: RBI currency-in-circulation data shows cash in the system has kept growing in absolute rupee terms (from roughly Rs 11.8 lakh crore in 2013 to about Rs 35-40 lakh crore currently), even as UPI processes 16+ billion transactions a month -- India has empirically been a 'both grow' market rather than a straight digital-displaces-cash market, concentrated in rural/semi-urban cash dependence that isn't disappearing on a 3-year view. The real multi-year risk is narrower and more specific: bank-driven offsite-ATM network rationalization and increasingly aggressive re-tender pricing as large PSU banks (having just seen SBI extract a marquee 10-year deal) negotiate harder on unit economics -- a genuine, not fabricated, margin risk, and consistent with why quality_score_pctile sits at a mediocre 45.5. At ~14.5-14.7x trailing earnings and ~1.8-1.9x book against a 12.5-13.2% ROE, the stock isn't table-pump-your-fist cheap on trailing numbers alone, but it is cheap against what FY27 guidance implies for a normalized earnings base, and the -47.8% one-year drawdown looks like it is extrapolating FY26's air-pocket into a permanent growth-rate reset rather than pricing the already-resolved SBI catalyst and the credible reacceleration guide.
recommendation_rationale: This is a genuine judgment call, not a clean override in either direction. The quant model's Sell verdict is driven almost entirely by 12-month price momentum (-47.8%) reflecting a real, not fake, FY26 growth/margin collapse (revenue +2.6%, PAT -18.5%, working capital deterioration, FCF negative on an all-in basis) -- those are legitimate quality concerns and the below-median quality percentile (45.5) is earned, not stale. But the single largest driver of that collapse -- the delayed SBI cash-outsourcing contract -- is now resolved and live (Jan 2026, Rs 1,000cr/10yr), Q4 FY26 already shows a sharp sequential recovery (services revenue record, margin +280bp QoQ, PAT +38% QoQ), management has issued a credible double-digit FY27 growth guide, the PE-sponsor overhang has fully cleared, and capital-return signals (9x-oversubscribed buyback, insider stake increase, net-cash balance sheet) read as management confidence rather than distress. On balance I lean Hold for an existing position: selling into a trough that coincides with a resolved catalyst and a management guide for reacceleration risks realizing the loss right before the recovery it is designed to capture. But I would not call this comfortable -- if Q1-Q2 FY27 fail to show growth reverting toward the guided range, the Sell case strengthens materially, and this genuinely could go either way, which is why I am flagging it rather than presenting it as settled.
summary: CMS Info Systems, India's #1 cash-logistics player (~46% ATM cash-management share), had a real, not cosmetic, bad FY26: revenue growth collapsed to 2.6% (from a 9.1% 3-year CAGR), EBITDA fell 5.2%, PAT fell 18.5% to Rs 303 crore, and working-capital quality deteriorated, driven mainly by repeated delays to a large SBI cash-outsourcing contract (~Rs 150cr revenue hit), an AGS-exit-related disruption in the offsite-ATM market, and one-off wage costs. The key fact for an existing holding: the SBI contract (Rs 1,000cr/10-year, 5,000 ATMs) went live in January 2026, Q4 FY26 already shows a sharp sequential recovery (services revenue record-high, margin +280bp QoQ, PAT +38% QoQ), and management guides FY27 total revenue growth of 13-17% (services 17-21%). The PE-sponsor (Baring/Sion) fully exited by mid-2025 with no residual overhang, CEO Rajiv Kaul has been raising his personal stake, and the company just completed a 9x-oversubscribed Rs 168 crore buyback plus a Rs 5.25/share dividend off a net-cash balance sheet. India's currency-in-circulation continues to grow in absolute terms despite UPI's scale, so the cash-logistics TAM is not obviously collapsing on a 3-year view, though bank ATM-network rationalization and tougher re-tender pricing are real structural risks. At ~14.5-14.7x trailing earnings against a depressed FY26 base, the -47.8% drawdown looks more like the market extrapolating one bad, largely-resolved year into a permanent growth reset than a re-rating on new structural information. Judgment call: Hold, with genuine two-way risk that the Principal should be aware of.

reverse_dcf_judgment: [INFERENCE/OPINION] At ~14.5-14.7x trailing PE and a ~3.3% (ex-acquisition) FCF yield off a deliberately depressed FY26 earnings base (PAT down 18.5% YoY), the market's implicit assumption is close to 'FY26's 2.6% growth is closer to the new steady state than a one-off trough' -- i.e., pricing something in the low-single-digit perpetual-growth range with little to no credit for the SBI contract ramp or the AIoT/managed-services mix-shift. I think that's more pessimistic than the evidence supports: the largest single drag (the delayed SBI deal) is now a signed, live, 10-year revenue stream, Q4 FY26 already shows the operating recovery in the actual numbers (not just guidance), and a business generating high-configuration ROCE (17.6-22.5% depending on source) with a net-cash balance sheet and management credibly guiding 13-17% FY27 growth should not be underwritten at a multiple implying near-zero durable growth. On a normalized FY27 earnings base (if guidance is even directionally met), the effective forward multiple compresses meaningfully below the trailing 14.5x -- suggesting the -47.8% drawdown has overshot the fundamental deterioration. That said, this is not a slam-dunk value case: quality percentile (45.5) and the FY26 working-capital/FCF deterioration are real, not cosmetic, and if FY27 growth again disappoints (repeating the pattern of over-optimistic prior guidance), the current multiple would look expensive rather than cheap. Net: a defensible, not obvious, undershoot -- the kind of setup where 'Hold and watch the next two quarters' is more honest than a confident directional call either way.
